name: Masahiro Hamazaki
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 1964 Emperor's Cup with Yawata Steel at age 24, and played in the inaugural Japan Soccer League season in 1965 at age 25.
early_history_summary: Born in Osaka, Hamazaki played youth football at Katsuyama High School and Meiji University before joining Yawata Steel (later Nippon Steel) as a goalkeeper. He won the Emperor's Cup with the club in 1964 and was part of the inaugural Japan Soccer League season in 1965.
primary_early_advantage_tags: university football, corporate team system, JSL founding
evidence_summary: Hamazaki progressed through the Japanese university football system (Meiji University) to a corporate team (Yawata Steel), winning the Emperor's Cup in 1964 and joining the inaugural JSL in 1965. No family background or early advantage information was documented in reviewed sources. His career benefited from Japan's corporate football structure of the era.
starting_point: Born in Osaka, Japan in 1940; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Died in October 2011 at age 71 in Kitakyushu, Japan; final role: retired footballer who had played 100 JSL games for Yawata Steel/Nippon Steel.

trajectory.event: Won the Emperor's Cup with Yawata Steel, a major national football title.

Died of ruptured varicose veins in Kitakyushu, Japan.

name: Anne Heggtveit
milestone_by_age_26: Won the Holmenkollen Giant Slalom in Norway in 1954 at age 15 as the youngest-ever winner; later won Olympic gold in slalom at age 21 in 1960.
early_history_summary: Born into a deep skiing family in Ottawa, Heggtveit started skiing at age 2 under her father Halvor, a Canadian cross-country champion. By age 7 she was the senior ladies combined champion at Camp Fortune, and she joined the Canadian National Team at age 9. She won the Holmenkollen Giant Slalom at 15 and Olympic gold at 21.
family_context_summary: Born to Halvor Heggtveit, a Canadian cross-country skiing champion of Norwegian descent who qualified for the 1932 Olympics, and Doll Clark. The family owned Heggtveit Sporting Goods in Ottawa, specializing in ski equipment.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a Canadian cross-country champion and Olympic qualifier; uncle Bud Clark raced Nordic at the 1936 Olympics; uncle Bruce crafted Anne's first pair of skis. Father served as her primary mentor and convinced her she could be Canada's first Olympic gold medalist in skiing.
primary_early_advantage_tags: skiing family, father as coach, early start age 2, prodigy, sporting goods business, Norwegian heritage
evidence_summary: Anne Heggtveit was born into a multi-generational skiing family in Ottawa—her father was a Canadian cross-country champion, her uncle an Olympian, and the family owned a ski equipment store. She started skiing at age 2, was competing by 7, and joined the Canadian National Team at 9. By 15, she won the Holmenkollen Giant Slalom as the youngest-ever winner, and at 21 she won Canada's first Olympic skiing gold medal at the 1960 Squaw Valley Games.
starting_point: Born in Ottawa to a Norwegian-heritage skiing family; father Halvor was a Canadian cross-country champion and the family owned a ski equipment store.
current_position: Retired from competition since 1960; later worked as an accountant and photographer; resides in the United States; member of the Order of Canada (1976).

trajectory.event: Won the senior ladies combined championship at Camp Fortune, marking the start of her competitive skiing career.
Became the youngest-ever winner of the Holmenkollen Giant Slalom in Norway.
Competed at the Cortina d'Ampezzo Winter Olympics despite injuries in prior years.
Won Canada's first Olympic gold medal in alpine skiing (slalom) at Squaw Valley; also claimed world championship titles in slalom and combined.
Awarded the Lou Marsh Trophy as Canada's outstanding athlete of the year.
Received the inaugural John Semmelink Memorial Award.
Made a member of the Order of Canada.

family_context_summary: Born in Yerevan, Armenian SSR, Soviet Union in 1953. Further family background not documented in reviewed sources.
evidence_summary: Sarkissian followed a standard Soviet academic path: university graduation at 23, doctoral studies completed at 25, and assistant/associate professorship at Yerevan State University. evidence_summary: Taimiņa graduated from the University of Latvia in 1977 and taught mathematics there for 20 years. name: Luc Montagnier
milestone_by_age_26: Was a research assistant at the Faculty of Sciences of Paris from 1955; completed a small thesis at age 21. HIV discovery came in the 1980s and Nobel Prize in 2008. No material milestone by age 26 found.
early_history_summary: Montagnier studied at the University of Poitiers and then became an assistant at the Faculty of Sciences at the Sorbonne. He obtained his PhD in Medicine in 1960 at age 28. His Nobel Prize-winning HIV discovery came in the 1980s.
family_context_summary: Born in Chabris, central France. His father had a hobby laboratory and gave him a microscope with time-lapse camera. His grandfather died of colon cancer in 1947, which inspired his interest in medicine.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father provided a home laboratory setup with a time-lapse movie camera and microscope, enabling early research. No evidence of professional scientific background in the family.
evidence_summary: Montagnier did a small thesis on phototaxy of chloroplasts at age 21 using a home laboratory setup provided by his father. He was a research assistant at the Sorbonne from 1955 and obtained his PhD in Medicine in 1960 at age 28. His Nobel Prize-winning co-discovery of HIV came in 1983 when he was 51. No material, independently verifiable milestone by age 26 was found; his early career consisted of standard academic positions.

name: Ildikó Újlaky-Rejtő
milestone_by_age_26: Won the World Junior foil championship in 1956 at age 19 (and again in 1957), followed by World Championship team gold in 1959 at age 22 and Olympic team silver in 1960 at age 23.
early_history_summary: Born deaf in Budapest with scoliosis, Rejtő started fencing at age 15 when her father enrolled her in lessons to help straighten her back. She learned by reading written instructions from coaches. Despite her disabilities, she won the World Junior foil championship at 19 and went on to become one of the greatest fencers in history.
family_context_summary: Born in Budapest, Hungary, and Jewish. She was born deaf and had scoliosis since her teenage years. Her father enrolled her in fencing lessons to help straighten her back.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father enrolled her in fencing for therapeutic reasons related to scoliosis; no evidence of family fencing background. A physical education teacher at her school, Kovácsné Nyári Magda (herself a fencer), recommended fencing.
primary_early_advantage_tags: deaf, scoliosis, therapeutic start, Hungarian fencing system, written instruction
evidence_summary: Rejtő was born deaf with scoliosis in Budapest and began fencing at 15 for therapeutic reasons, learning through written instructions from coaches. Despite these barriers, she won the World Junior foil championship at 19 (1956) and again at 20 (1957), then World Championship team gold at 22 and Olympic team silver at 23. Hungary's deep fencing tradition and club system (Újpesti TE) provided the pipeline, but her rapid rise from a late start with significant disabilities was remarkable.
starting_point: Born deaf in Budapest, Hungary in 1937 to a Jewish family; father enrolled her in fencing at age 15 to treat scoliosis.
current_position: Retired Hungarian two-time Olympic and five-time World Champion foil fencer; living in Budapest at age 89.

trajectory.event: Won the World Junior foil championship, her first major international title.

Won Olympic individual bronze and team silver at the Mexico City Olympics.
Won Olympic team bronze at the Montreal Olympics, her fifth Olympic Games.

name: John le Carré
milestone_by_age_26: Taught French and German at Eton College from 1956-58 at ages 25-27; first novel 'Call for the Dead' published in 1961 at age 30; international fame with 'The Spy Who Came in from the Cold' in 1963 at age 32. No material milestone by age 26 found.
early_history_summary: Born David Cornwell in Poole, England, le Carré did National Service in the Intelligence Corps (1950-52), studied modern languages at Lincoln College, Oxford (1952-56), and taught at Eton College (1956-58) before joining MI5 in 1958. His first novel was published at 30.
family_context_summary: Born in Poole, England to Ronnie Cornwell, an erratic businessman who was frequently bankrupt and imprisoned for fraud, and Olive Glassey. His father's criminal lifestyle and financial instability shaped his childhood. He was abused by his father.
parent_family_domain_summary: No evidence of literary or intelligence background in the family. Father was a conman whose lifestyle created instability; le Carré's espionage career was self-initiated.
evidence_summary: Le Carré served in the Intelligence Corps during National Service, studied at Oxford while spying for MI5, and taught at Eton from 1956-58. He joined MI5 in 1958 and MI6 in 1960. His first novel was published at 30 and his breakthrough 'The Spy Who Came in from the Cold' at 32. By age 26 he was a schoolteacher at Eton; no material, independently verifiable creative or professional milestone by age 26 was found.

name: Stefan Johansson
milestone_by_age_26: Won the Swedish karting championship in 1973 at age 17; won the British Formula Three championship in 1980 at age 24 and made his Formula One debut the same year.
early_history_summary: Born in Växjö, Sweden, Johansson started karting at age 8 with help from his father Roland, a weekend saloon car racer who ran a body repair shop. He won the Swedish karting championship at 17, progressed through Formula Ford, and won the British F3 championship at 24 before entering Formula One.
family_context_summary: Born in Växjö, Sweden. Father Roland Johansson ran a body repair shop and raced saloon cars on weekends (VW Beetle, Mini, ex-Alan Mann Escort). The family was not wealthy; Stefan later slept in his car and struggled to afford food while racing in England.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a successful touring/saloon car racer who introduced Stefan to motorsport from childhood. Stefan grew up in racing paddocks and started driving karts at age 8 with his father's enthusiastic support.
primary_early_advantage_tags: father racer, karting from age 8, body repair shop, Swedish racing tradition, financial hardship
evidence_summary: Johansson grew up in Växjö with a father who raced saloon cars and ran a body repair shop, giving him early immersion in motorsport. He started karting at 8, won the Swedish championship at 17, and progressed through Formula Ford to win the British F3 title at 24. His father's racing connections and hands-on support were critical, but the family lacked financial resources—Stefan slept in his car and struggled to eat while racing in England. He made his F1 debut with Shadow in 1980.
starting_point: Born in Växjö, Sweden; father ran a body repair shop and raced saloon cars on weekends, providing early immersion in motorsport.
current_position: Former F1 and CART driver; won 24 Hours of Le Mans in 1997; now a motorsport executive running Johansson Motorsports in Indianapolis.

name: Pentala Harikrishna
milestone_by_age_26: Won the World Under-10 Chess Championship in 1996 at age 10; became India's youngest grandmaster in 2001 at age 15; won the World Junior Championship in 2004 at age 18.
early_history_summary: Born in Guntur, Andhra Pradesh, India, Harikrishna learned chess at age 4 from his grandfather Ranga Rao, a village chess enthusiast. He won the World Under-10 Championship at 10, became a grandmaster at 15 (India's youngest at the time), and won the World Junior Championship at 18.
family_context_summary: Born to Nageswara Rao and Padmavathi, agriculturists from Prathipadu village near Guntur, Andhra Pradesh. The family had financial difficulties; a doctor once advised quitting chess at age 6 due to headaches. His maternal grandfather Ranga Rao was his first chess teacher and biggest influence, traveling unreserved on trains with the young Harikrishna to tournaments.
parent_family_domain_summary: Grandfather Ranga Rao was a village chess enthusiast who recognized Harikrishna's talent when the boy solved a chess problem at age 5 that adults had missed. Grandfather became his first coach and dedicated supporter, despite family pressure to focus on studies. Parents were agriculturists with no chess background.
primary_early_advantage_tags: grandfather as coach, village background, prodigy, financial hardship, early start age 4, Indian chess boom
evidence_summary: Harikrishna learned chess at age 4 from his grandfather in a village near Guntur, India. Despite financial hardships and a doctor's advice to quit at age 6, he won the World Under-10 Championship at 10 and became India's youngest grandmaster at 15 in 2001. His grandfather was his first coach and most dedicated supporter, traveling unreserved on trains to tournaments. The family were agriculturists with no chess background, making Harikrishna's rise largely self-driven with grandfather's mentorship. He later received formal training from G.K. Narayana, Shiv Prasad, and Yevgeniy Vladimirov.
starting_point: Born to agriculturist parents in Guntur, Andhra Pradesh, India; learned chess at age 4 from his maternal grandfather in a village setting.
current_position: Active chess grandmaster; peak world ranking No. 10 (November 2016) with peak Elo rating of 2770; currently ranked around No. 60 globally.
